predictions.explanation:
Jason’s prediction was that “in the next five years” there would be roughly $1–2 trillion deployed into AI-related data centers. The episode aired on August 9, 2025, and the quote in transcript form clearly frames this as a five‑year forward-looking claim about cumulative investment.([speakai.co](https://speakai.co/podcast-transcription/all-in-podcast/openais-gpt-5-flop-ais-unlimited-market-chinas-big-advantage-rise-in-socialism-housing-crisis/?utm_source=openai))

As of the current date (November 30, 2025), less than one year of that five‑year window (Aug 2025–Aug 2030) has elapsed, so the actual 5‑year cumulative spend is not yet known. Existing figures and reports are mainly *forecasts*, not realized totals. For example, Dell’Oro Group and others project that AI-related data center and infrastructure capex over the next several years will exceed $1 trillion, and some estimates (e.g., Brookfield, McKinsey) put AI data center or compute-related capex in the multi-trillion-dollar range by 2030, suggesting Jason’s order-of-magnitude estimate is plausible or even conservative.([prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/ai-infrastructure-spending-forecast-to-be-over-a-trillion-dollars-over-the-next-five-years-according-to-delloro-group-302210735.html?utm_source=openai))  But because these are projections rather than final, realized numbers, we cannot yet say whether the world actually *did* invest $1–2 trillion in AI data centers during the full five-year period he specified.

Therefore, the prediction’s correctness cannot currently be determined and is **inconclusive (too early)**.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction explicitly refers to *"the coming years"* and says socialism will *"sweep over this nation"* (the U.S.), which implies a multi‑year horizon beyond the few months that have passed between the podcast date (August 9, 2025) and now (November 30, 2025). That time frame has clearly not elapsed, so the claim can’t be fairly judged yet.

Substantively, current indicators do **not** yet show socialism as nationally *dominant*:
- National polling still shows most U.S. voters prefer a free‑market system over socialism; one 2025 survey finds 71% of likely voters say a free‑market economy is better than socialism and only 12% say socialism is better. ([rasmussenreports.com](https://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/politics/partner_surveys/71_of_voters_reject_socialism?utm_source=openai))
- Gallup‑based reporting indicates that while support for capitalism is at a historic low (about 54% viewing it favorably), socialism remains less popular overall, with roughly 39% favorability nationwide. ([foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/media/us-support-capitalism-sinks-new-low-gallup-poll?utm_source=openai))
- Within the Democratic Party, socialism has become relatively popular (about two‑thirds of Democrats view it positively), but Republicans and independents remain largely negative, so it is far from a cross‑partisan national consensus. ([yournews.com](https://yournews.com/2025/09/08/3843606/gallup-poll-finds-democrats-favor-socialism-over-capitalism-for-first/?utm_source=openai))
- Politically, the U.S. House of Representatives recently passed a resolution explicitly denouncing socialism, with a large bipartisan majority voting in favor—hardly evidence of socialism having already “swept” national politics. ([time.com](https://time.com/7335809/house-denounces-socialism-mamdani-trump-meeting/?utm_source=openai))

However, because the prediction’s horizon is “coming years,” it is too early, as of late 2025, to decide definitively whether socialism will eventually “sweep over” the U.S. and produce the broad unhappiness Friedberg fears. The appropriate classification is therefore **inconclusive (too early to tell)**, even though available data so far do *not* show the predicted dominance of socialism nationwide.

predictions.explanation:
Key facts about the scenario:

- The race being discussed is the 2025 New York City mayoral election, in which New York State Assembly member Zohran Mamdani ran for mayor.
  - Mamdani won the Democratic primary on June 24, 2025, defeating Andrew Cuomo.
  - He then won the general election on November 4, 2025, and is mayor‑elect, scheduled to take office on January 1, 2026. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_York_City_Democratic_mayoral_primary?utm_source=openai))
- Eric Adams initially ran for a second term but **withdrew** from the race in September 2025 (though his name remained on the ballot). Cuomo, after losing the Democratic primary, continued as an independent candidate and did not withdraw. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_York_City_mayoral_election?utm_source=openai))

How this maps to the prediction:

1. **"Assuming Adams or Cuomo do not withdraw ... Mamdani will win"**  
   - This is explicitly conditional on *neither* Adams nor Cuomo withdrawing. In reality, Adams did withdraw his campaign in September 2025. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_York_City_mayoral_election?utm_source=openai))  
   - Because the stated assumption failed, we cannot directly evaluate the truth of Gavin’s conditional claim as formulated. The world followed the "Adams pulls out" branch, where he did *not* say what he expected to happen.

2. **"If he wins and fully implements his socialist policies, they will be epic failures within a few years and will quickly end socialism"**  
   - As of November 30, 2025, Mamdani has **not yet taken office** as mayor; his term starts January 1, 2026. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zohran_Mamdani?utm_source=openai))  
   - Consequently, he has not had any meaningful opportunity as mayor to “fully implement” his stated municipal socialist agenda (free buses, rent freezes, city‑run groceries, etc.), so their success or failure cannot yet be judged. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zohran_Mamdani?utm_source=openai))  
   - The prediction further specifies a horizon of “within a few years.” Only a few months have elapsed since the August 2025 podcast date, and zero time has passed in office, so that timeframe has not even begun, let alone expired.
   - Available evidence actually points to ongoing or even growing socialist organizing rather than a "quick end": the Democratic Socialists of America report about 90,000 members as of November 2025, up from a trough in 2024, and Mamdani’s mayoral win is described as a major DSA victory. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Socialists_of_America?utm_source=openai))  Still, this does **not** falsify the prediction, because the claimed causal test (full implementation over a few years) has not yet occurred.

Because:
- The first clause is explicitly conditional on an assumption that did **not** hold (Adams did withdraw), and
- The second, more substantive clause concerns outcomes **“within a few years” after full implementation of policies**, a period that has not yet begun and certainly has not elapsed,

there is not yet enough real‑world data to determine whether Gavin’s overall prediction is right or wrong.

Therefore, the appropriate classification as of November 30, 2025 is: **inconclusive (too early to tell).**

predictions.explanation:
**What the prediction required**  
Normalized: *If* the Fed cuts rates by about 50 bps sometime in Sept–Nov 2025, *then* U.S. CPI inflation will **subsequently** rise back to 3.0–3.9% year‑over‑year (a “3‑handle”) within the following months.

**What actually happened so far**

1. **Fed policy in Sept–Nov 2025**  
   The FOMC cut the target federal funds range by 25 bps on **September 17, 2025** (to 4.00–4.25%) and again by 25 bps on **October 29, 2025** (to 3.75–4.00%). That’s a cumulative **50‑basis‑point cut within the Sept–Nov window**, so the *condition* (“if the Fed cuts ~50 bps in Sept–Nov”) has been met. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Federal_Open_Market_Committee_actions))

2. **Inflation behavior around that time**  
   * CPI year‑over‑year was **2.7%** in June and July 2025. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2025/consumer-price-index-rose-2-7-percent-for-the-12-months-ending-june-2025.htm?utm_source=openai))  
   * It then rose to **2.9% in August 2025**. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2025/consumer-prices-up-2-9-percent-from-august-2024-to-august-2025.htm?utm_source=openai))  
   * The **September 2025** CPI report (released October 24) shows the all‑items CPI up **3.0% year‑over‑year**, i.e., already a “3‑handle.” ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_10242025.htm?utm_source=openai))

   So by September, inflation *had* risen back to 3.0%.

3. **Data gap after the full 50 bps of cuts**  
   The last 25‑bp cut that completes the “~50 bps” path occurred on **October 29, 2025**. The months **“subsequent”** to that are November 2025 onward. However, because of the October–November 2025 government shutdown, the **October CPI was not collected and will not be released**, and the **November CPI report (which will partly impute October) has not yet been published as of November 30, 2025**. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/schedule-us-economic-data-delayed-by-government-shutdown-2025-11-28/?utm_source=openai))  
   That means we do **not yet have any CPI data for a month that is clearly *after* the full 50‑bp cut path is in place.**

**Why the prediction is labeled ‘inconclusive’**

- The **antecedent** (“Fed cuts ~50 bps in Sept–Nov”) is satisfied: 25 bps in September + 25 bps in October. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Federal_Open_Market_Committee_actions))  
- We do see CPI at **3.0% in September**, which matches the “three‑handle” level Jason talked about. But that 3.0% reading:
  - Largely reflects price movements **before** the October 29 cut, and 
  - Occurs when only **half** of the eventual 50‑bp Sept–Nov easing (the Sept 17 cut) had taken place.
- The normalized version of the prediction you provided, however, specifies that CPI will **“subsequently rise back”** to 3–3.9% **after** the roughly 50‑bp easing in the Sept–Nov window. To test that strictly, we must look at months *after* the full 50‑bp path is in effect (i.e., November 2025 and beyond). Because of the data shutdown and normal release lag, those CPI figures are **not yet available** as of November 30, 2025. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/schedule-us-economic-data-delayed-by-government-shutdown-2025-11-28/?utm_source=openai))

Given this, we can’t yet say—on the basis of actually released post‑cut data—whether **“after the ~50‑bp cuts”** inflation is at 3–3.9%. His *general intuition* that inflation would get back to a 3‑handle is already borne out by the September print, but the **specific conditional, as normalized (tied to the full Sept–Nov 50‑bp easing), cannot yet be definitively judged.**

Hence the verdict: **"inconclusive" (too early to fully evaluate),** with the caveat that the available data so far are directionally consistent with his claim.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction specified a window of **~18 months from August 2025**, i.e. until around **February 2027**, for “a Gen‑4 reactor [in the U.S.] deployed or started production.” As of **November 30, 2025**, that deadline has **not yet arrived**, so we cannot know whether it will ultimately be met.

Current evidence shows several U.S. Generation IV / advanced reactor projects are **under development or early construction**, but not yet deployed or producing power:

- **Project Pele microreactor (DoD/BWXT)** – DoD and DOE report that ground was broken at Idaho National Laboratory in 2024 and that the transportable high‑temperature gas reactor is being built by BWXT, with assembly starting in 2025 and potential operation at INL as early as **2026**; it is expected to be the **first Generation IV reactor to generate electricity in the U.S.** ([defense.gov](https://www.defense.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/3915633/dod-breaks-ground-on-project-pele-a-mobile-nuclear-reactor-for-energy-resiliency/?utm_source=openai))  
- **Kairos Power Hermes 1 & 2 (fluoride‑salt‑cooled reactors)** – The NRC has issued construction permits for Hermes 1 (non‑power demonstration) and, more recently, for Hermes 2 units that Kairos describes as the first electricity‑producing Gen IV reactors permitted for construction in the U.S., but these units are **not yet operating**. ([powermag.com](https://www.powermag.com/nrc-approves-construction-of-first-electricity-producing-gen-iv-reactor-in-the-u-s/?utm_source=openai))  
- **TerraPower Natrium (sodium‑cooled fast reactor, Wyoming)** – Non‑nuclear site work started in 2024, with nuclear construction expected after an NRC construction permit targeted for 2026 and operation around 2030; as of late 2025 it has **not begun nuclear island construction or operation**. ([powermag.com](https://www.powermag.com/doe-allocates-first-round-of-haleu-to-five-u-s-advanced-nuclear-reactor-developers/?utm_source=openai))  

These timelines suggest it is **plausible** that at least one Gen IV project (e.g., Project Pele or a Hermes/Natrium unit) could be under construction or even operating by early 2027, but that outcome lies in the **future** relative to the current date. Because the 18‑month window has not elapsed and we lack information from beyond November 2025, we **cannot yet determine** whether Friedberg’s prediction will ultimately be correct.

Therefore, the appropriate classification as of now is **“inconclusive (too early).”**

predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, the full multi‑quarter trajectory Ben described has not played out long enough to be definitively confirmed or falsified, and early data cut in different directions from his story.

**1. Tariff revenues have not yet shown the predicted drop.**  
Ben expected that after an initial spike, U.S. tariff revenues would decline as demand fell. Instead, 2025 data so far show *rising* and then persistently high tariff collections:
- Treasury figures indicate customs duties climbed from about $17–24 billion per month in April–May to roughly $28–29 billion in June–July, with August hitting about **$31.4 billion**, the largest monthly haul of 2025 at that point.
  ([foxbusiness.com](https://www.foxbusiness.com/politics/august-tariff-collections-reach-31-4b-largest-monthly-haul-so-far-2025?utm_source=openai))  
- Subsequent reports for **October 2025** show another record customs‑duty take of about **$31–31.4 billion**, and year‑to‑date tariff revenue near **$195 billion**, far above the prior year and with officials projecting even higher totals if current policies persist.
  ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-posts-284-billion-october-budget-deficit-report-impacted-by-shutdown-2025-11-25/?utm_source=openai))  
So far, there is no sign yet of the clear revenue decline he predicted, but his timeframe (“over the next several quarters”) extends into 2026, so the revenue leg of the forecast isn’t fully testable yet.

**2. Inflation has not clearly fallen due to tariff‑driven demand destruction.**  
Ben argued that falling demand would bring inflation down. In reality, U.S. CPI inflation fell to about **2.3% year‑over‑year in April 2025** and then moved *up* into the high‑2% to ~3% range by mid‑2025, with reports noting inflation “quickened” in August and reached **around 3.0%** in September. ([usinflationcalculator.com](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/u-s-inflation-eases-some-as-cpi-hits-7-7-in-october/100023292/?utm_source=openai))  
As of late November 2025, widely cited indicators still place U.S. inflation at roughly **3%**, not meaningfully below pre‑tariff levels, and commentary often treats the new tariffs as **adding** to price pressures, not relieving them. ([forecasts.org](https://www.forecasts.org/economic-indicator/inflation.htm?utm_source=openai))  
Thus, the mechanism “tariffs → weaker demand → clearly lower inflation” is not yet visible in the data, but again, the horizon is multi‑quarter and could still evolve.

**3. The Fed has started cutting rates, but for different stated reasons and before the predicted setup.**  
Ben said the Fed would cut rates *after* tariff revenue and demand dropped and inflation came down. What has actually happened:
- The Fed held the federal funds target range at **4.25–4.50%** through June and July 2025. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/monetary20250730a.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- On **September 17, 2025**, it cut rates by **25 bps** to **4.00–4.25%**, explicitly citing moderating economic activity, slower job gains, and rising downside risks to employment, while noting that **inflation had “moved up” and remained somewhat elevated**. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20250917a.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- On **October 29, 2025**, it cut again, directing a target range of **3.75–4.00%**. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20251029a1.htm?utm_source=openai))  
Fed communications and coverage emphasize labor‑market softness and risk management—cutting *despite* still‑elevated or slightly higher inflation and acknowledging tariffs as an inflationary factor—rather than as a response to a tariff‑induced collapse in demand and inflation. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/f1d4522b-331e-45d5-b676-24dc5b8e3c92?utm_source=openai))

**Assessment:**  
- Core elements of Ben’s causal chain (tariff revenues falling, demand‑driven disinflation leading to rate cuts) are **not** supported by current data: revenue is at record levels, inflation is roughly flat to slightly higher than pre‑tariff lows, and the Fed has already begun cutting rates primarily due to labor‑market concerns while inflation remains above target.  
- However, because his forecast explicitly referenced the “next several quarters,” and we are only a few months beyond the August 2025 tariff shock with much of that horizon still ahead, it is too early to say with certainty that the longer‑run pattern he described cannot emerge.

Given this mix—early evidence running against his mechanism, but insufficient elapsed time relative to his stated horizon—the fairest classification as of November 30, 2025 is **"inconclusive" (too early), albeit trending away from his scenario rather than toward it.**

predictions.explanation:
Available evidence lets us evaluate parts of the prediction but not the core claim about its ultimate impact on the U.S.–China AI race.

1. **"Hard to stop" and ongoing, meaningful smuggling**  
After Washington tightened export controls, multiple investigations found that *at least* about $1 billion worth of Nvidia’s banned B200/H100/H200 chips entered China via gray/black‑market channels in roughly a three‑month window in 2025, showing both substantial volume and the difficulty of fully halting flows. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/nvidia-ai-chips-worth-1-billion-entered-china-despite-us-curbs-ft-reports-4150736?utm_source=openai))  A 2025 Center for a New American Security (CNAS) working paper, using probabilistic modeling and open‑source evidence, estimates that on the order of tens to hundreds of thousands of export‑controlled AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 (median ≈140,000), concluding that smuggling “has likely been occurring at a scale that significantly undermines U.S. attempts” to restrict access and that enforcement capacity is insufficient. ([cnas.org](https://www.cnas.org/press/press-release/new-paper-warns-ai-chip-smuggling-to-china-may-undermine-u-s-national-security-interests?utm_source=openai))  U.S. Justice Department cases in 2024–2025 (e.g., against ALX Solutions and Bitworks) describe ongoing schemes that routed Nvidia H‑class chips through third countries like Malaysia and Singapore to reach Chinese buyers, confirming that smuggling continues despite prosecutions. ([aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2025/8/6/us-charges-chinese-nationals-with-illegally-shipping-nvidia-chips-to-china?utm_source=openai))  These points support the *descriptive* part of the prediction: smuggling persisted at a meaningful level and has been hard to stop completely.

2. **Scale relative to U.S. hyperscaler deployments**  
Even if smuggling reached several billion dollars’ worth of chips over a year, this is still small compared with the legitimate AI build‑out by major cloud providers. TrendForce projects that total 2025 capex for eight large cloud service providers (including U.S. hyperscalers like AWS, Google, Microsoft, and Meta) will exceed **$420 billion**, with GPU procurement a central driver. ([trendforce.com](https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20251013-12741.html?utm_source=openai))  Bank of America analysis cited 2025 capex plans of about **$105 billion for Amazon** and **$64–72 billion for Meta** alone, a large share of which is AI infrastructure. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/2025-ai-capex-outlook-remains-strong-nvidia-broadcom-top-picks-bofa-4037847?utm_source=openai))  Individual high‑end Nvidia H100‑class chips were selling for roughly **$25,000–30,000** each in 2024, implying that U.S. hyperscalers’ annual AI‑chip orders correspond to many tens of billions of dollars in hardware. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopper_%28microarchitecture%29?utm_source=openai))  By contrast, press reports on China’s black market emphasize that projects built around smuggled B200/H100/H200 racks are “much smaller compared with mega clusters of data centres being built by tech giants around the world,” aligning with the claim that this channel is material yet modest relative to top‑tier hyperscaler deployments. ([chinastrategy.org](https://www.chinastrategy.org/2025/07/24/nvidia-ai-chips-worth-1bn-smuggled-to-china-after-trump-export-controls/?utm_source=openai))  So the **relative‑scale** part of the prediction is broadly supported by current data.

3. **Whether smuggling is “decisive” in the U.S.–China AI capability race**  
Where the prediction becomes harder to judge is the causal claim that this smuggling **“will not be decisive”** for the overall U.S.–China AI race. CNAS and related analyses argue that smuggled chips could already account for a non‑trivial fraction of China’s AI compute—on the order of ~10% of its 2024 training capacity in their median scenario—and that this may grow as legal channels tighten, warning that such flows “significantly undermine” the intended effects of U.S. controls and merit being treated as a national‑security priority. ([cnas.org](https://www.cnas.org/press/press-release/new-paper-warns-ai-chip-smuggling-to-china-may-undermine-u-s-national-security-interests?utm_source=openai))  That language underscores that serious experts see smuggling as strategically important. At the same time, U.S. and allied hyperscalers still appear to be deploying substantially more frontier‑class compute overall, and China’s leading firms are also turning to other workarounds like training models in overseas data centers that legally host Nvidia hardware, which further complicates attributing future capability gaps to smuggling versus other channels. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/96fe9898-a3a4-4a33-be1d-da06bdb6cb2b?utm_source=openai))  

Crucially, as of late 2025 there is **no settled “outcome”** of the U.S.–China AI capability race, nor a rigorous counterfactual showing how that outcome would differ absent smuggling. Analysts can say smuggling is significant or worrying, but not whether it *ultimately* will or will not be “decisive” in shaping long‑run relative capabilities.

Because:
- the *empirical* components of the prediction (continued, hard‑to‑stop smuggling at ~$1B‑scale over a few months; volumes still smaller than U.S. hyperscaler deployments) are strongly supported by current reporting, **but**
- the *core forward‑looking claim* about its non‑decisiveness for the long‑term U.S.–China AI race cannot yet be tested,

there is not enough evidence to say the overall prediction has clearly come true or failed. On balance, this makes the prediction **inconclusive** rather than clearly right or wrong at this time.

It’s too early to score this prediction.

Chamath’s claim is about **2030**: “I think the estimate is in 2030, 30 million electric vehicles.” The current date is **November 30, 2025**, so we are still about 4–5 years away from the target year. We can assess trajectory but not the final outcome.

As context, U.S. EV stock (battery electric + plug‑in hybrids) has been growing quickly but is still far below 30 million:

- The International Energy Agency estimated about **3 million** electric cars in the U.S. fleet in 2023.
- Various industry and analyst forecasts (BloombergNEF, IEA, major automakers) project continued rapid growth toward the late 2020s, with cumulative EVs plausibly reaching the tens of millions by 2030, but the exact 2030 figure will depend on policy, charging build‑out, consumer adoption, and automaker product plans.

However, because **2030 has not yet occurred**, we cannot say whether the U.S. will actually have “on the order of 30 million” EVs by that time. The most accurate status classification today is therefore *inconclusive (too early)*.

predictions.explanation:
There isn’t enough verifiable information on how quickly 2025 All‑In Summit scholarship applications were processed to judge Jason’s claim.

What we can see:
- The public scholarship links used in mid‑ and late‑2025 episodes (e.g., via the bit.ly URL in the show notes) just redirect to an application page that is not accessible through open web archives; none of the mirrored episode descriptions mention a specific response-time promise.([listennotes.com](https://www.listennotes.com/podcasts/all-in-with/openais-gpt-5-flop-ais-ve7BPjzq-RQ/?utm_source=openai))
- The best third‑party description of the 2025 scholarships—Vanity Fair’s long piece on the 2025 All‑In Summit—confirms the existence and structure of the paid “scholarship application” passes (around $1,500) but does **not** describe how fast applicants heard back or whether decisions typically came within a week.([vanityfair.com](https://www.vanityfair.com/news/story/all-in-is-coming-for-everyone-else))
- Historical user reports from earlier years (2023–2024) on Reddit show multiple people saying they applied for All‑In Summit scholarships and either had not heard back at all months later or were still waiting without any clear timeline, which cuts against a consistent one‑week turnaround in those years.([reddit.com](https://www.reddit.com/r/TheAllinPodcasts/comments/16gdh5q?utm_source=openai)) However, those anecdotes pre‑date the 2025 process Jason was talking about and don’t prove that 2025 timelines were the same.
- For a different All‑In event (the 2025 Holiday Party), their own event page only says scholarship applications are “reviewed on a rolling basis,” with no commitment to a one‑week SLA, suggesting they generally avoid promising a specific turnaround publicly.([accelevents.com](https://www.accelevents.com/e/all-in-holiday-party?utm_source=openai))

Because there’s no reliable, aggregated data on 2025 scholarship response times—and only scattered, older anecdotes that point in different directions—we can’t confidently say whether applicants in 2025 “typically” heard back within a week. The prediction therefore can’t be judged definitively as right or wrong with the evidence currently available.
